title: Vector helpers
text:
Vector helpers are evaluated once per group on whole columns. Use them as mutate(), filter(), and summarize() arguments. They follow R’s NA rules: a summary returns NA when its input has an NA unless naRm: true, ranks keep NA, and cumulative functions stay NA after the first NA.
The first argument is the input column. A string there is a column name. It can also be col('x'), another helper, or a row closure. Later arguments are values. ->map(fn ($value, $r) => ...) transforms a helper’s result row by row.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Summaries



Helper
Value




n()
Rows in the group


n_distinct('x', 'y')
Distinct values or combinations


sum, mean, median
As in R


sd, var_ (alias variance)
Sample statistics (n − 1)


quantile('x', 0.9), iqr('x')
Type 7 quantiles, R’s default


min, max
Smallest and largest values


first, last, nth('x', 2)
Values by position, with default:


any, all
Logical summaries with NA logic



With the phit extension loaded, mean, sd, var_, median, and quantile use it. Without it, they run in PHP. The test suite checks both against R.

Window functions







Helper
Value

row_number(), row_number('x')

min_rank, dense_rank
Ranks; wrap the column in desc() to reverse


percent_rank, cume_dist
Ranks scaled to [0, 1]


ntile('x', 4)
Buckets of near-equal size


cumsum, cumprod, cummin, cummax, cummean

cumall, cumany

A new id each time the value changes

A window function evaluated in another order




PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv') |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->school === 'school-01') |>
    arrange('study_hours') |>
    mutate(
        prev: lag('score'),
        change: lag('score')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : round($r->score - $prev, 2)),
        running_mean: cummean('score'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('score')),
        pct: percent_rank('score'),
        quartile: ntile('score', 4),
    ) |>
    select('study_hours', 'score', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile') |>
    head(8);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv'))
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->school === 'school-01')
    ->arrange('study_hours')
    ->mutate(
        prev: lag('score'),
        change: lag('score')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : round($r->score - $prev, 2)),
        running_mean: cummean('score'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('score')),
        pct: percent_rank('score'),
        quartile: ntile('score', 4),
    )
    ->select('study_hours', 'score', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile')
    ->head(8);

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]) |>
    mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),
        any_flag: when_any(fn ($r) => $r->state === 'CA', fn ($r) => $r->visits === 0),
    );


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]))
    ->mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),

Strings and dates
text: phplyr re-exports phibble’s stringr and lubridate functions. They build expressions, so they work in memory and, where a SQL translation exists, on database tables. Their results are checked against stringr 1.6.0 and lubridate 1.9.5.

title: Strings and dates
text:
Strings
As in stringr, a pattern is a regular expression. fixed('a.b') matches the text literally, and regex('ab', ignoreCase: true) sets options.







Function
Value




str_detect(x, p, negate:), str_starts, str_ends
Whether the pattern matches


str_count(x, p)
Number of matches


str_extract(x, p)
The first match, or NA


str_extract_all(x, p), str_split(x, p)
A list per row (a list-column)


str_split_i(x, p, i)
The i-th piece; negative counts from the end


str_replace(x, p, r), str_replace_all
Replace the first or every match; \1 refers to a group


str_pad(x, width, side:, pad:)
Pad to a width


str_trunc(x, width, side:, ellipsis:)
Truncate with an ellipsis


str_to_title, str_to_upper, str_to_lower
Change case


str_squish, str_trim(x, side)
Remove whitespace


str_length, str_sub(x, start, end)
Length and substrings



Strings are UTF-8. str_length(), str_sub(), str_pad(), and the other functions count UTF-8 characters, and the case functions change accented letters too.
str_replace, str_pad, and str_split have the names of PHP built-ins. In a file that imports them, write \str_replace() for the built-in.

title: Strings and dates
text:
Dates and times







Function
Value




ymd, dmy, mdy, ymd_hms, dmy_hms, mdy_hms (tz:)
Parse text; failures give NA


parse_date_time(x, ['Ymd HMS', 'dmY HMS'])
Parse with lubridate orders


year, month, day, yday, quarter, hour, minute, second
Parts


wday(x, weekStart:)
Day of the week; Sunday is 1 unless weekStart: 1


floor_date(x, unit), ceiling_date, round_date
Round to 'hour', '15 minutes', 'week', 'month', and so on


seconds(n) … years(n)
Periods: col('d')->add(months(1))


difftime(x, y, units:)
The difference as a number


with_tz(x, tz), force_tz(x, tz)
Change the displayed zone, or the zone itself


today(tz:), now(tz:)
The current date or time



The parsing functions return UTC date-times unless tz: names a zone, as in lubridate. PHP’s default time zone does not change the result. with_tz() keeps the instant and changes the zone it is shown in, and force_tz() keeps the clock time and changes the zone.
On a database table, a function without a SQL translation for that database loads the rows and runs in PHP, as Databases and expressions describes.
Month and year arithmetic that lands on a date that doesn’t exist, such as January 31 plus one month, gives NA, as in lubridate. Subtracting dates gives days, and subtracting datetimes gives seconds. Date columns stay dates through these functions. Phibble\Expr\Clock::freeze() fixes today() and now() in tests.

title: Models
text:
lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer() pass the table to phit’s Phit\fit_lm(), Phit\fit_glm(), Phit\fit_lmer(), and Phit\fit_glmer(). phplyr adds no model code of its own. phit reads factor levels from the table, builds the model matrix from an R formula, and fits the model.
Two implementations of these functions are supported, and phplyr calls both the same way:
CI runs phplyr’s test suite with each one. Both runs compare lm() and glm() coefficients with R’s and lmer() fixed effects with lme4’s.
phit-polyfill has the same functions, arguments, and results for the models, with these differences:
With neither installed, the four functions throw a RuntimeException that names the missing phit function.
Other named arguments go to phit’s function unchanged. phit’s documentation lists them and the formula syntax it accepts.

title: Models
Grouping
text:
group_by() sets the grouping columns. Selectors work, named arguments group by a computed column, and _add: true adds to the existing groups. _drop: false keeps groups for unused factor levels, so summarize() and count() return them with n() = 0, as dplyr does. ungroup() removes grouping, or only the named columns.
Groups are ordered like dplyr’s: sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. filter(), mutate(), summarize(), and the slice functions work within groups. _by: groups for a single call and returns an ungrouped table.

title: Grouping
Porting an R script
text:
This page takes a typical R analysis of the schools data and translates it to PHP with phplyr and phit. The analysis reads a CSV file, cleans and reshapes it, summarizes it, and fits a linear, a logistic, and a random-intercept model. Both scripts ran when the documentation was built. The output under each script is what it printed.
The data is schools.csv. The R script needs dplyr, tidyr, and lme4. The PHP script needs phplyr and the phit extension for the models.

title: Porting an R script
text:
What changed in translation

Loading. read.csv() becomes DataFrame::fromCsv(). phibble infers column types like readr.
Pipes. On PHP 8.5, R’s |> stays |>. Each function returns a closure that the pipe applies. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the pipeline becomes a method chain: phplyr($t)->filter(...), ending with ->get().
Column references. Bare names become strings, or col('x') inside expressions. score - prior_score becomes col('score')->sub(col('prior_score')). A row closure, fn ($r) => $r->score - $r->prior_score, also works.
Conditions. case_when(x < 4 ~ "low", .default = "high") becomes case_when([col('x')->lt(4), 'low'], default: 'high').
Renaming in select. select(prior = prior_score) becomes select(['prior' => 'prior_score']).
Column sets. c(prior, final) becomes ['prior', 'final'].
Models. lm(), glm(), and lmer() take the same formulas. They return arrays with columns (R’s coefficient names), coefficients, standard errors, and fit statistics instead of model objects, so coef() and fixef() become array reads.
Printing. DataFrames print in tibble’s format. R rounds printed numbers to significant digits; phibble does the same.

Because the PHP pipeline uses col() expressions instead of closures, it also runs unchanged on a database table from Phibble\tbl(). See Databases and expressions.

title: phplyr
text: phplyr is a library of functions for filtering, transforming, summarizing, joining, and reshaping tables of data in PHP. Each function takes a table and returns a new one, so a sequence of them reads as a pipeline from the raw data to the result. The functions and their arguments follow R’s dplyr and tidyr packages, and the test suite compares their results with R’s.

title: phplyr
phplyr
text:
phplyr and phibble
The tables come from phibble, which Composer installs with phplyr. phibble reads CSV files, database queries, and PHP arrays into a typed, immutable DataFrame. Its methods, such as filter(), mutate(), groupBy(), summarize(), arrange(), and join(), are the operations every phibble table implements. They take closures, arrays of column definitions, and phibble expressions.
phplyr is built on those methods and adds:

dplyr’s functions and arguments, including grouped window functions such as lag() and min_rank(), across(), column selectors such as starts_with(), join_by() conditions, and the slice_*() family.
tidyr’s pivoting, completing, splitting, nesting, and list-column functions.
janitor’s clean_names(), remove_empty(), get_dupes(), and tabyl().
Adapters that pass a table to phit’s lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer().

A phplyr pipeline runs on any phibble table: the in-memory DataFrame, a database table from Phibble\tbl(), which runs the pipeline as SQL, and Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable, which runs it in Polars through the phpolars extension.

title: phplyr
text:
Install
composer require phpstats/phplyr
phplyr supports PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5, and requires the mbstring and PDO extensions. Pipelines written with the pipe operator |> need PHP 8.5.
The optional features are statistical models (the phit extension or phit-polyfill), native descriptive statistics (phit), the Polars backend (phpolars), janitor’s transliteration of names (intl), and database tables (a PDO driver). Installation in Getting started describes the requirements and each optional feature.
Compatibility and limitations lists the PHP and backend details and the dplyr features phplyr does not have.

title: Gallery

Compatibility and limitations
text:
phplyr supports PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. CI tests all three on Linux.
The pipe operator |> is PHP 8.5 syntax. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the same pipelines are method chains, or calls to pipe(). Every function works on all three versions.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
phplyr supports PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. CI tests all three on Linux.
The pipe operator |> is PHP 8.5 syntax. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the same pipelines are method chains, or calls to pipe(). Every function works on all three versions.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Requirements
phplyr requires the mbstring extension. Composer installs these with phplyr:

phibble (phpstats/phibble 0.3, 0.4, or 0.5), which provides the tables. phibble requires PHP’s PDO extension.
symfony/polyfill-php84, which provides PHP 8.4 functions on PHP 8.3.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Optional extensions



Extension
Enables




phit
lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer(), and native mean(), sd(), var_(), median(), and quantile()


phpolars
phibble’s PolarsTable backend


intl
Transliteration in make_clean_names() and clean_names() that matches R’s janitor


A PDO driver (SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL)
Database tables through Phibble\tbl()



Without phit, the descriptive helpers run in PHP, and the model functions throw a RuntimeException that names the missing function. phit-polyfill defines the model functions in PHP. See Models. Without intl, make_clean_names() transliterates with iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Backends
A phplyr function calls the methods of phibble’s Table contract, so a pipeline runs on any table that implements it:

Phibble\DataFrame holds the data in PHP memory.
Phibble\tbl($pdo, 'table') builds SQL for SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL. A function given a PHP closure, and an expression without a SQL translation, runs the query so far, loads the rows, and continues in memory. Databases and expressions lists those expressions.
Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable belongs to phibble and runs pipelines in Polars through the phpolars extension. A closure step converts the data to a DataFrame and back.

The test suite runs about 120 pipelines on both DataFrame and PolarsTable and requires the same columns, types, groups, and rows from each.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Not supported

Bare column names and tidy evaluation. Columns are strings, and expressions are closures, helpers, or col() expressions.
mutate(_keep: 'used') and _keep: 'unused' with closures. These work with expression arguments such as col('x')->mul(2), whose columns phplyr can read. A PHP closure does not expose the columns it reads, so phplyr throws an InvalidArgumentException.
cur_data() and cur_data_all(), which dplyr has deprecated. Use pick().
Data frame columns and across(.unpack). pack() makes a column of named arrays.
The scoped _at, _if, and _all variants, such as mutate_at(). Use across().
janitor’s adorn_*() functions and three-way tabyl().

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Differences in behavior

_by sorts groups. dplyr keeps the order of first appearance for .by. phplyr sorts by key, as it does for group_by().
Strings are UTF-8. String functions count UTF-8 characters.
Date-times parse to UTC unless a function is given tz:, whatever PHP’s default time zone is, as in lubridate.
Models return arrays. lm() and the other model functions return phit’s result array, with R’s coefficient names in columns, in place of a model object.

title: Coming from dplyr
text: phplyr keeps dplyr’s and tidyr’s function names, argument names, and results. This page lists the differences that come from PHP syntax. Compatibility and limitations lists the dplyr features phplyr does not have.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Syntax translation
In R, functions are chained with %>% or |>. In PHP 8.5, they are chained with |>. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, they are methods of a chain: phplyr($t)->filter(...)->arrange(...). The table below shows single calls.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Conventions

Dot-arguments keep the dot as a leading underscore, and a multi-word name is camelCase after it: .by is _by: and .keep_all is _keepAll:. See Underscored arguments.
Positions are 1-based, as in R: pull(1) is the first column, pull(-1) the last, and slice(1, 3) the first and third rows of each group.
var() is var_(), because var is a reserved word in PHP. variance() is an alias.
summarise() and summarize() are the same function, as in dplyr.
count(), min(), max(), rename(), and other functions have the names of PHP built-ins. In a file that imports them, write \count() for the built-in. Imports lists them.
Group order follows dplyr: groups are sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. _by also sorts groups (dplyr keeps first-appearance order for .by).

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Underscored arguments
phplyr’s parameters are camelCase, like the rest of the phpstats family. Every argument that dplyr or tidyr writes with a dot keeps it here as a leading underscore, and a multi-word name is camelCase after the underscore. There are sixteen options. recode() also names its first parameter $_x, after dplyr’s .x:

Most of the verbs that take one are variadic. A named argument to a variadic function lands in the same string-keyed array as the columns the call creates, so without the prefix the option would always win and a column of that name would be unreachable. dplyr and tidyr use the dot for the same reason. With the prefix, both work:

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$t |> mutate(m: mean('x'), _by: 'g');
$t |> mutate(by: 1);


phplyr($t)->mutate(m: mean('x'), _by: 'g');
phplyr($t)->mutate(by: 1);



The first call computes m within each group of g. The second makes a column called by.
The prefix is the only spelling an option has. An unprefixed named argument is always data, so mutate(before: 'id') makes a column called before rather than placing the new columns. A prefixed name that is not an option for that verb is an error naming the ones that are.
Every other argument is camelCase, as in the rest of the phpstats packages. dplyr and tidyr write these without a dot: naRm:, orderBy:, namesFrom:, namesTo:, withTies:, and the rest.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
phplyr options and phibble methods
phplyr functions and phibble methods both take and return phibble tables, so a pipeline can use both. phibble’s methods have their own conventions:

A phibble method takes an array: $df->mutate(['z' => $expr]), $df->groupBy(['g']), $df->arrange([['x', 'desc']]). A phplyr function takes named arguments: mutate(z: ...), group_by('g'), arrange(desc('x')).
phibble methods have no underscored options. Grouping is a separate method call, and summarise(array $aggregates, ?string $groups) takes the .groups value as a second argument.
A phplyr helper such as mean('x') returns a Phplyr\Vec that holds a Phibble\Expr tree, the kind phibble’s expression functions build. phplyr passes the tree to the table. A database table compiles it to SQL where a translation exists and otherwise loads the rows and evaluates it in PHP, as Databases and expressions describes.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
across() functions
R passes a vector to every across() function. PHP closures have no such convention, so phplyr decides what a function receives:

A phplyr helper passed as a first-class callable, such as mean(...) or lag(...), is called with each column’s name.
In summarize(), any other closure receives the column’s values as a list.
In mutate(), a closure receives one value at a time. If its first parameter is typed array, it receives the whole column instead.

title: Development
text:
Documentation
The site is a Quarto project in docs/. Code examples live in docs/examples/*.php. bin/docs-examples runs each one with docs/data as the working directory and writes docs/examples/_<name>.md with the code and its output, which the pages include. Rendering never executes PHP.
An example uses |>, and docs/examples/<name>.chain.php beside it is the same example as a method chain. bin/docs-examples runs both and fails if their output differs. The page shows the two in tabs labeled “PHP 8.5+” and “PHP 8.3–8.4”, with the output once. bin/docs-examples needs PHP 8.5, and it loads phit from .ext/libphit.dylib for the model examples.
Most examples leave out the require line and the imports, and bin/docs-examples adds them before it runs the code. An example that requires vendor/autoload.php itself is a complete script. It runs as written, so a missing import fails the run, and the page shows the whole file. The first example and the pages in the Examples section (docs/examples/<slug>.qmd, with their code in docs/examples/pages/) are complete scripts.
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/docs-examples   # refresh example output
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/render-docs     # examples, quarto render, publish to docs/

Getting started
text:
composer require phpstats/phplyr



PHP 8.3, 8.4, or 8.5. CI tests all three on Linux. Pipelines written with the pipe operator |> need PHP 8.5, and method chains run on all three.
The mbstring extension, which phplyr requires.
The PDO extension, which phibble requires.

Composer installs phibble (0.3, 0.4, or 0.5), which provides the tables, and symfony/polyfill-php84, which provides PHP 8.4’s functions on PHP 8.3.



Statistical models. lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer() call phit’s model functions. Either of two implementations provides them, and phplyr calls both the same way:

The phit extension, written in Rust. phplyr works with phit 0.1 and later. CI builds it from phit’s main branch.
phit-polyfill, the same functions in PHP, for systems where the extension cannot be installed. CI tests phplyr with phit-polyfill 0.3. Install it with composer require phpstats/phit-polyfill. Models describes what it leaves out.

Native descriptive statistics. With the phit extension loaded, mean(), sd(), var_(), median(), and quantile() call phit’s statistics functions. Without the extension, including with phit-polyfill, they run in PHP and give the same results.
Polars. The phpolars extension provides phibble’s PolarsTable, which runs a pipeline in Polars. See Compatibility and limitations.
Transliteration of names. With the intl extension, make_clean_names() and clean_names() transliterate non-ASCII names the way R’s janitor does. Without it, they use iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s. See janitor.
Database tables. Phibble\tbl() runs a pipeline as SQL through PDO. It needs the PDO driver for the database: SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL. See Databases and expressions.

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
Imports
phplyr’s functions are namespaced functions in Phplyr. Import the ones a file uses with use function:
use Phibble\DataFrame;
use function Phplyr\{phplyr, filter, mutate, group_by, summarize, arrange, desc, n, mean};
A method chain needs phplyr() and the helpers it calls, such as n(), mean(), and desc(). The table functions are the chain’s methods, so they don’t need importing.
Some phplyr functions have the same names as PHP built-in functions. In a file that imports one of them, the bare name calls phplyr’s function. Write a leading backslash to call the built-in, as in \count($array).



phplyr functions
Where they are documented




count, rename
Single-table functions


min, max
Vector helpers


abs, sqrt, exp, log, log10, round, floor
Expressions


str_replace, str_split, str_pad
Strings and dates


extract, chop, pack, unpack
tidyr



A file that doesn’t import these names is not affected.

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
Pipelines
A table function such as filter(...) returns a closure that takes a table and returns a new one. A pipeline applies such closures in order.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


The pipe operator |> calls the closure on its right with the value on its left:
$out = $schools |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80) |>
    arrange(desc('score'));


phplyr($table) starts a method chain. Each method calls the phplyr function of the same name with the same arguments. A chained method is camelCase, so group_by() is ->groupBy() and n_groups() is ->nGroups(). get() returns the table:
$out = phplyr($schools)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    ->arrange(desc('score'))
    ->get();



The two forms give the same result, and the documentation shows both.
A method chain stays a chain while each method returns a table. These functions return something else, and the chain returns that value:







Functions
Return




pull(), group_vars(), group_size(), group_indices(), group_rows(), group_split(), group_map()
An array


n_groups()
An integer


setequal()
A boolean


show_query()
The SQL string


lm(), glm(), lmer(), glmer()
phit’s result array



echo prints a chain’s table without get(). ->pipe($closure) applies a closure of your own and continues the chain with its result.
pipe() applies closures in order on every PHP version:
$out = pipe($schools, filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80), arrange(desc('score')));

title: Getting started
section: Columns, row closures, and vector helpers

title: Getting started
text:
Named arguments and options
Functions that create columns name them with PHP named arguments: mutate(total: ...), summarize(n: n()). An option that dplyr writes with a leading dot, such as .by, is written with a leading underscore, such as _by:. Any other named argument is a column, so mutate(_before: 'id') places the new columns and mutate(before: 1) makes a column called before. Underscored arguments lists them.
PHP does not allow positional arguments after named ones. Put across() and other positional arguments first: summarize(across(...), n: n()).

title: Getting started
text:
Printing and inspecting
echo prints a table. glimpse() prints one line per column and returns the table unchanged, so it can sit inside a pipeline. pull('x') returns a column as a PHP array, and $table->toRows() returns every row as an array.

title: Performance
text: phplyr is a thin layer. Each function calls one or two methods of the table it is given, so the backend determines how fast a pipeline runs. This page reports timings for phibble’s shared benchmark workloads on DataFrame and SQLite, and for three phplyr pipelines on DataFrame, PolarsTable, and SQLite, and gives guidance on choosing a backend.

title: Performance
text:
Method
bench/harness.php runs each workload twice: as a phplyr pipeline, and as the same calls made directly on the table. bench/generate.php writes the data. It is the same generator and seed as phibble’s bin/bench, so the two harnesses time identical data:

events.csv: 1,000,000 rows of id, key (10,000 distinct values), g (8 labels), x (float, about 2% NA), and t (datetime).
dims.csv: 100,000 rows of key, label, and w.

php bench/generate.php 1000000
php bench/harness.php --backend=dataframe --runs=3
php bench/harness.php --backend=sqlite --runs=3
Each timing includes collect(), so lazy backends do their work inside the timer. The numbers below are medians of three runs on an Apple Silicon Mac with PHP 8.5 and phibble fa978f6.

title: Performance
text:
phplyr’s overhead
At 100,000 rows, the phplyr pipeline and the direct calls differed by at most 5% on every workload and backend, which is within run-to-run noise. Grouped slices, pivot_*(), and complete() build on the same table methods and carry the same small overhead.

title: Performance
text:
Choosing a backend

In-memory DataFrame suits data that fits in memory, up to a few million rows. Expression arguments are the fastest form: a grouped summary with mean('x') runs about four times faster than the same summary written as closures, because phibble computes it in one pass without building a table per group.
A database table (Phibble\tbl()) avoids loading the data into PHP. With expressions, filter() and summarise() run in the database, and only the result reaches PHP, so memory stays small. This is the right choice when the data lives in a database or doesn’t fit in memory. For data already in memory, a data frame is faster: these timings exclude loading, and reading the 1M-row CSV into a data frame takes about 1.4 seconds. Pipelines that return every row (mutate(), arrange(), unfiltered joins) spend most of their database time transferring rows to PHP.
Closures on a database table load all rows first and then run in memory. Use col() expressions and phplyr’s helpers to keep the work in SQL.
SQLite columns need declared types. PDO binds values as strings. In an untyped column, SQLite stores them as text and compares numbers as text.
PolarsTable (phibble’s Polars backend, on the phpolars extension) runs the pipeline in Polars, 10 to 100 times faster than DataFrame, and pays mainly for bringing rows back into PHP. See below.

title: Performance
text:
PolarsTable
bench/backends.php times three phplyr pipelines on DataFrame, PolarsTable, and SQLite, and checks that all three backends return the same rows. It is adapted from phpolars’ benchmark script. The pipelines are:

A: filter, join a store lookup, two-key summarise, then a ranking window.
B: grouped lag(orderBy:), cumsum(), and a share of the group total over all rows.
C: pipeline A with a closure in filter().

Times are the best of three runs through collect(), on an Apple M5 Ultra with Homebrew PHP 8.5, phibble 0.3.0, and Polars 0.55.2 at two threads. In every case the three backends returned the same rows. The full results, with all repeat timings and version details, are in benchmarks/backends-results.json.
bench/backends.R runs pipelines A and B with dplyr 1.2 on the same data, and checks that dplyr’s row counts and column sums match phplyr’s. Its results are in benchmarks/dplyr-results.json. Pipeline C has no dplyr version, because its closure is PHP code.










Pipeline, 1M rows

dplyr runs these pipelines in compiled code. On A, which reduces the data before collecting, PolarsTable (0.05 s) and dplyr (0.07 s) take about the same time. On B, which returns every row, dplyr is the fastest by a wide margin.
The operations themselves are fast in Polars. Most of PolarsTable’s time goes to converting results back to PHP values: about 0.2 seconds per million rows of plain columns, plus about 0.5 seconds per million values of a datetime column, because each value becomes a PHP DateTimeImmutable. A pipeline that returns every row of a table with a datetime column can therefore be slower on PolarsTable than on DataFrame. In phibble’s harness, mutate() and left_join() returning 1M rows took 1.3 seconds on PolarsTable against 0.3 seconds on DataFrame.
A closure makes PolarsTable convert the data to a DataFrame and back, which costs about a second per million rows. Pipeline C runs its closure step that way.
Use PolarsTable when a pipeline reduces the data before collecting (summaries, filters, distinct(), or a join followed by a summary), when it chains several steps, or when the data starts in Polars: PolarsTable::fromPolars(Phpolars\read_csv($path)) skips phibble’s CSV parse. Keep the pipeline in expressions so every step stays in Polars.

title: Databases and expressions
text:
phplyr’s helpers build inspectable expressions whenever their arguments are column names, literals, or other helpers. col('x') refers to a column, and methods combine expressions with operators:
filter(col('price')->mul(1.1)->gt(100), col('brand')->isIn(['a', 'b']))
mutate(margin: col('price')->sub(col('cost'))->div(col('price')))
mutate(dev: col('score')->sub(mean('score')))      // mean() recycles per group
The operator methods are add, sub, mul, div, mod, pow, neg, eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, and, or, not, isNa, isIn, between, and desc. Scalar helpers include round, abs, sqrt, exp, log, log10, floor, ceiling, is_na, as_int, as_float, as_string, as_bool, paste, and paste0. Several of these names shadow PHP built-ins in files that import them. The string and date helpers are expressions too.
An expression is a Phibble\Expr tree. phplyr passes it to the table. The in-memory DataFrame evaluates it with dplyr’s semantics, and a database table compiles it to SQL. A helper given a PHP closure still works, but it is evaluated in PHP.
mutate(_keep: 'used') and _keep: 'unused' need expression arguments, because phplyr reads the columns an expression uses from the tree.

mutate(margin: col('price')->sub(col('cost'))->div(col('price')))
mutate(dev: col('score')->sub(mean('score')))      // mean() recycles per group

title: Databases and expressions
janitor
text: phplyr has the single-table functions from R’s janitor package. The test suite compares each one with janitor 2.2 output from tests/r/janitor.R.

title: janitor
text:
Clean names
clean_names() renames every column of a table, and make_clean_names() applies the same rules to a list of strings. The rules follow janitor’s defaults:

% becomes percent, # becomes number, and quotes are dropped.
Accented and non-Latin characters are transliterated to ASCII: Café becomes cafe, straße becomes strasse, and αβγ becomes abg.
Spaces and punctuation become single underscores, and leading and trailing ones are dropped.
Case changes split words: camelCaseVar becomes camel_case_var, and HTMLParser becomes html_parser. Digits stay attached to their word.
A name that would start with a digit gets an x prefix, and an empty name becomes x.
A repeated name gets _2, _3, and so on, in order of appearance.

Transliteration uses ext-intl, which gives the same results as janitor’s stringi. Without ext-intl, phplyr falls back to iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s.
make_clean_names(['First Name', 'first_name', '% Done', '1st Place']);
// ['first_name', 'first_name_2', 'percent_done', 'x1st_place']

pipe($survey, clean_names());

title: janitor
text:
Remove empty rows and columns
remove_empty() drops rows and columns that are entirely NA. Pass 'rows' or 'cols' to drop only one kind. With cutoff below 1, a row or column is kept when its share of non-NA values is above the cutoff. A cutoff works with only one of 'rows' and 'cols'. An empty string is a value, as in R.

title: janitor
text:
Duplicates
get_dupes('email') returns the rows whose values in the given columns appear more than once. The result has the given columns first, then dupe_count, then the other columns. Rows are sorted by dupe_count (descending) and then by the given columns. With no columns, every column is used. A grouped table keeps its groups, but duplicates are found across the whole table.

title: janitor
text:
Frequency tables
tabyl('g') counts the values of one column. The result has the values, n, and percent. When the column has NAs, valid_percent gives each share with NA left out. showNa: false drops the NA row instead.
tabyl('g', 'h') counts pairs of values. It has one row per value of g and one column of counts per value of h. An NA in h is counted in the NA_ column, and an empty string in the emptystring_ column.
Values are sorted as in dplyr’s count(), with NA last. Factors keep their level order, and showMissingLevels: false leaves out unused levels.
pipe($people, tabyl('region'));
pipe($people, tabyl('region', 'smoker', showNa: false));
janitor’s adorn_*() functions and three-way tables are not included.

title: Single-table functions
Single-table functions
Single-table functions
Single-table functions
tidyr
text: The tidyr functions use tidyr’s argument names. Arguments that start with a dot in tidyr keep the dot here as a leading underscore, camelCase after it: .names_sep on pack() is _namesSep:. See Underscored arguments.

title: tidyr
tidyr
text:
Missing combinations and values
complete() adds missing combinations of the given columns and fills other columns with NA, or with values from fill:. A column name expands to its unique values (a factor to its levels), nesting() keeps only combinations that occur, and a named list supplies the values. It works within groups. expand() returns only the combinations, and crossing() and expand_grid() build a new table from lists.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]) |>
    complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]))
    ->complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);



# A tibble: 6 × 3
  shop  month sales
  <chr> <int> <int>
1 north     1    10
2 north     2     0
3 north     3    12
4 south     1     0
5 south     2     7
6 south     3     0
fill() carries values down or up over NA within groups (_direction: 'down' | 'up' | 'downup' | 'updown'). drop_na() drops rows with NA in the given columns, and replace_na() replaces NA per column.

Every value from the smallest to the largest in steps of period



tooFew and tooMany handle pieces that don’t fit, as in tidyr.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$t = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Ada Lovelace', 'tags' => 'math,code'],
    ['id' => 2, 'name' => 'Grace Hopper', 'tags' => 'navy'],
]);

echo $t |> separate_wider_delim('name', ' ', names: ['first', 'last']);
echo "\n", $t |> select('id', 'tags') |> separate_longer_delim('tags', ',');
echo "\n", $t |> select('id', 'name') |> unite('label', 'id', 'name', sep: ': ');


$t = DataFrame::fromRows([

Joins, binding, and set operations
Joins, binding, and set operations
Joins, binding, and set operations
text:
join_by()
join_by() builds dplyr’s join specifications. A string is an equality on the same column name, ['a' => 'b'] maps names, and a comparison of two col() expressions compares x’s column (left) with y’s (right). Every condition must hold.
join_by('id', col('t')->ge(col('start')), col('t')->lt(col('end')))
join_by('id', between('t', 'start', 'end'))        // start and end are y's columns
join_by('id', closest(col('t')->ge(col('start'))))  // the latest start at or before t
join_by(within('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))         // x's interval inside y's
join_by(overlaps('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))
For inequality, rolling, and overlap joins, keep defaults to dplyr’s behavior: equality keys are merged and the columns in other conditions are kept from both tables. keep: false is an error for these joins. Database tables run them in SQL, except right and full rolling joins, which load the rows.
nest_join() keeps every row of x and adds a list-column (name:, default 'data') holding each row’s matching rows of y as a table.
